---
title: "Getting started with tidy data"
---

Use this guide if you need to publish statistics on Explore Education
Statistics (EES) and are new to tidy data. It explains what tidy data is, then
follows one table through to a finished data file and metadata file, with
optional R and Python examples.

Start with a copy of one small table. Identify the headings that describe
groups, then sketch how those groups could become columns. You can work out
the structure before choosing how to produce the file.

EES is the service DfE uses to publish official statistics. When you publish a
release, users can read your commentary, build their own tables and charts from
your data, and download the data files you upload. Those data files need to be
in a tidy format so that EES, and the people using your data, can work with
them.

The [Open Data Standards](ud.qmd) are the full reference, including exceptions
and accepted values. If you want to make files available through the API, the
[API data standards](api-data-standards.qmd) apply as well.

## What is tidy data

The numbers in the examples on this page have been created for illustration only.

In a tidy data file, each row is one observation and each column is one
variable. Tables made for reading on screen often spread a variable across
several columns instead.

This table of primary pupils puts sex in the column headings:

| Region | Male | Female |
|---|---|---|
| North East | 13100 | 11900 |
| North West | 36100 | 33900 |

Here is the same data as tidy data, with sex in its own column and the numbers
in another:

| region_name | sex | pupil_count |
|---|---|---|
| North East | Male | 13100 |
| North East | Female | 11900 |
| North West | Male | 36100 |
| North West | Female | 33900 |

The tidy version is longer, but it is much easier for software to filter, sort
and add up, and it can hold more breakdowns without changing shape.

1. [Work through an example](#worked-example): rearrange the counts, add totals, then add the EES fields
2. [Decide which of your tables go into which file](#start-from-what-you-already-have)
3. [Prepare each data file](#prepare-the-data-file)
4. [Create a metadata file for it](#create-the-metadata)
5. [Check your files](#check-your-files) and [how they look in EES](#check-how-it-looks-in-ees)
6. [Use the checklists](#checklists) before you publish

## Worked example {#worked-example}

This example starts from one Excel-style table of pupil numbers. You can
download it as a [source CSV](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-source.csv).
We will follow the North East figures for 2022/23 through three stages:

1. [Rearrange the existing counts](#rearrange-existing-counts)
2. [Add totals and percentages](#add-totals-and-percentages)
3. [Add EES time and geography fields](#add-ees-fields)

### 1. Rearrange the existing counts {#rearrange-existing-counts}

The source has one row for each academic year and region. Here is the North
East row, with descriptive headings in place of the source's abbreviations:

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Source data extract"}

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| output: asis
source_data <- read.csv("../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-source.csv",
                        colClasses = "character", check.names = FALSE)
example_data <- read.csv("../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.csv",
                         colClasses = "character", check.names = FALSE)
example_meta <- read.csv("../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.meta.csv",
                         colClasses = "character", check.names = FALSE)
source_extract <- source_data[source_data$academic_year == "2022/23" &
                               source_data$region_name == "North East", ]
source_display <- source_extract[, c("region_name", "male_prim", "female_prim",
                                    "male_sec", "female_sec")]
source_display[-1] <- lapply(source_display[-1], as.integer)
knitr::kable(source_display, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Region", "Male primary", "Female primary",
                           "Male secondary", "Female secondary"),
             format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             caption = "North East, 2022/23: the starting row (year column omitted).")
```

:::

Here are the same four counts with sex and phase in their own columns. The
year is still 2022/23 for every row:

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Rearranged data extract"}

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| output: asis
extract <- example_data[example_data$time_period == "202223" &
                        example_data$region_code == "E12000001", ]
detail_extract <- extract[extract$education_phase %in% c("Primary", "Secondary") &
                           extract$sex %in% c("Male", "Female"), ]
detail_extract <- detail_extract[order(
  match(detail_extract$education_phase, c("Primary", "Secondary")),
  match(detail_extract$sex, c("Male", "Female"))
), ]
detail_display <- detail_extract[, c("region_name", "sex", "education_phase",
                                    "pupil_count")]
detail_display$pupil_count <- as.integer(detail_display$pupil_count)
knitr::kable(detail_display, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Region", "Sex", "Phase", "Pupil count"),
             format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             caption = "North East, 2022/23: the same counts rearranged (year column omitted).")
```

:::

The numbers have stayed the same. The sex and phase information has moved out
of the headings into columns. The region repeats because each row needs to
identify which pupils the number describes.

Read the first row as: "In the North East, there are 13,100 male primary
pupils." Each row describes one combination of place, sex and phase for that
year. This is what we mean by one **observation**.

#### Which headings are really categories?

The four count columns are `male_prim`, `male_sec`, `female_prim` and
`female_sec`. Each heading hides two pieces of information: the pupils' sex and
their education phase.

In EES, categories users choose from are called **filters**. Here they become
two columns, `sex` and `education_phase`.
Users can then pick sex and phase separately, for example all female pupils, or
female primary pupils. A single combined column with values like "Female
primary" would stop them doing that.

#### Which values are measures?

The numbers in the four columns are all pupil counts, so they go into one
`pupil_count` column. EES calls a measure like this an **indicator**.

We have now rearranged one source row into four rows, without adding any
figures. These tables show the reshaping step; we will add the fields EES
requires in stage 3.

### 2. Add totals and percentages {#add-totals-and-percentages}

The next step adds calculated values. These do not appear automatically when
you rearrange the data.

#### What totals do users need?

The source has no totals, so the example adds them:

- male plus female, as `sex = Total`
- primary plus secondary, as `All education phases` in `education_phase`
- the nine regions added together, as national rows for England

Only add up groups that do not overlap. Do not add a total to the rows that make
it up, and do not add percentages together.

This example also adds a `pupil_percent` indicator, showing the percentage of
pupils of each sex within the same year, location and phase. Counts and
percentages describe the same groups, so they sit in the same file as separate
columns.

There were 13,100 male and 11,900 female primary pupils in the North East in
2022/23, so 25,000 in total. The percentage for males is
13,100 / 25,000 × 100 = 52.4. Explain what each percentage is a percentage of
in your public data guidance.

#### What the tidy file looks like

After those decisions, each row of the data file shows the pupil count and
percentage for one year, location, phase and sex. Here are the North East rows
for 2022/23, without the time and geography columns:

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Finished data extract"}

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| output: asis
totals_display <- extract[order(
  match(extract$education_phase, c("Primary", "Secondary", "All education phases")),
  match(extract$sex, c("Male", "Female", "Total"))
), c("education_phase", "sex", "pupil_count", "pupil_percent")]
totals_display$pupil_count <- as.integer(totals_display$pupil_count)
totals_display$pupil_percent <- as.numeric(totals_display$pupil_percent)
knitr::kable(totals_display, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Phase", "Sex", "Pupil count", "Pupil percentage"),
             format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             caption = "North East, 2022/23: counts and percentages including totals (time and geography columns omitted).")
```

:::

The four detail rows now have five total rows alongside them, making nine
rows for the North East in 2022/23.

### 3. Add EES time and geography fields {#add-ees-fields}

So far, the captions have told us the year and place. In the data file, each
row needs that information in columns that EES recognises.

#### What is the time period?

The source's `academic_year` value of 2022/23 becomes `time_period` of
`202223`, with `time_identifier` of `Academic year`.
See the [time columns](ud.qmd#time-columns) for other formats.

#### What is the geography?

The North East rows need the region code as well as the name, along with
`geographic_level` and the country code and name. Each of the nine rows above
gets the same time and geography values:

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Time and geography fields"}

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| output: asis
location_columns <- c("time_period", "time_identifier", "geographic_level",
                      "country_code", "country_name", "region_code", "region_name")
location_display <- data.frame(
  column = location_columns,
  value = unlist(extract[1, location_columns], use.names = FALSE)
)
knitr::kable(location_display, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Column in the data file", "Value on each row"),
             caption = "Time and geography fields for North East pupils in 2022/23.")
```

:::

Look up codes rather than typing them in. In R, the
[dfeR package](https://dfe-analytical-services.github.io/dfeR/) has lookups for
common geographies, including
[`fetch_regions()`](https://dfe-analytical-services.github.io/dfeR/reference/fetch_regions.html)
for regions. If you don't use R, this example has a
[region lookup CSV](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-region-lookup.csv)
with the same codes.

The full source has 18 rows: two academic years for each of the nine English
regions. Applying these steps across the source, including the England totals,
produces the [finished data file](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.csv)
with 180 rows: two years, ten locations, three phase values and three sex values.

## Start from what you already have

Most teams start with a set of Excel tables from a previous release, or files
from a database or another team. Each table usually shows a few breakdowns of
the same figures, laid out for people to read on screen.

Before changing any data, list your tables and group them:

- Tables that describe the same thing, such as pupil numbers by sex in one table
  and pupil numbers by phase in another, can usually be combined into one tidy
  file.
- Tables about different things, such as pupil numbers and school finance, or
  figures with different populations, usually belong in separate files.

A good test is whether it would make sense to show the data side by side in one
table. The EES table tool, where users build their own tables, can only use one
data file at a time, so anything users will want to compare needs to be in the
same file. The [dataset design decisions](ud.qmd#dataset-design-decisions) go
through the common choices with examples.

## Fewer, larger files

Aim for a small number of larger tidy files rather than one file for every
table you used to publish.

A tidy file is machine readable and ready for the API, so anyone can analyse it
or load it into their own tools. From that one upload you can also:

- recreate your usual tables as featured tables in EES, which appear as ready
  made tables for users who want a quick view
- let users build any other table they need in the table tool, picking only the
  years, locations and breakdowns relevant to them
- make charts from the same data

This gives every kind of user a route into the data from a single original
upload. Users who rely on Excel, or only want a small part of the data, can get
a smaller table from EES without you producing and checking it as a separate
file. Your own quality assurance also focuses on fewer files.

## Prepare the data file

Include the [mandatory time and geography columns](ud.qmd#time-and-geography):
`time_period`, `time_identifier`, `geographic_level`, `country_code` and
`country_name`. Add the [columns for each geography level](ud.qmd#allowable-geographic-levels)
you use. This example needs `region_code` and `region_name`, which are left
empty on the national rows.

Use [harmonised names and categories](ud.qmd#common-harmonised-variables)
where they exist. These are the standard column names and values DfE uses
across publications, such as `sex` with `Male`, `Female` and `Total`. Follow the
guidance on [variable names](ud.qmd#variable-names) and
[indicator names](ud.qmd#indicator-names) for other columns.

Give the file a short, lower case [file name](ud.qmd#file-names) without
spaces or years, such as `pupil-enrolments.csv`, so you can reuse it each
release. Save it as a
[UTF-8 CSV](ud.qmd#how-to-export-data-with-utf-8-encoding) with one header row,
no title rows and no row numbers. Keep geography codes as text, and store
percentages as numbers, for example `52.4` rather than `0.524` or `52.4%`.

This example has no missing or suppressed values. In your own data, use the
[standard symbols](ud.qmd#data-symbols), for example `c` for confidential, `x`
for unavailable and `z` for not applicable, and never use zero in their place.
Everything in the file can be downloaded, so apply your disclosure control to
the data itself.

## Create the metadata file {#create-the-metadata}

Each data file comes with a **metadata file**, a small CSV that tells EES which
columns are filters and indicators, and how to display them. For example:

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Data column and display label"}

| Column in your data | Label displayed in EES |
|---|---|
| `pupil_count` | Number of pupils |

: How metadata labels the pupil-count column.

:::

The metadata connects the column name to that label. It also sets display
details such as units and decimal places.

The metadata file needs the same name as the data file plus `.meta`, for
example `pupil-enrolments.meta.csv`. It has one row for each filter and
indicator in the data file.

You can start from a [blank metadata template](../resources/open-data-standards/metadata-template.meta.csv),
which has the eight [mandatory metadata columns](ud.qmd#mandatory-ees-metadata-columns).

The [example metadata file](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.meta.csv)
has one row for each of the two filters and two indicators. The columns that
affect how this example displays are:

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Metadata settings"}

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| output: asis
knitr::kable(example_meta[, c("col_name", "col_type", "label", "indicator_unit",
                              "indicator_dp", "filter_default")],
             row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Selected metadata settings for the pupil example.")
```

:::

In this example:

- `col_name` matches the column headers in the data file exactly
- counts have no unit and 0 decimal places, percentages use `%` and 1 decimal place
- filter rows leave the indicator columns empty, and indicator rows leave the
  filter columns empty
- the optional `filter_default` column sets `All education phases` and `Total`
  as the default selections, see [aggregates and default filters](ud.qmd#aggregates-and-default-filters)
- time and geography columns do not need metadata rows

## Try the example code

If you want to try the transformation in code, you can download scripts that
turn the source table into the finished files. You do not need to run them to
follow the worked example above.

For the R version, download:

- [prepare-pupil-example.R](../resources/open-data-standards/prepare-pupil-example.R)
- [pupil-source.csv](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-source.csv)

For the Python version, download:

- [prepare-pupil-example.py](../resources/open-data-standards/prepare-pupil-example.py)
- [pupil-source.csv](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-source.csv)
- [pupil-region-lookup.csv](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-region-lookup.csv)

You can compare what the scripts produce with the finished
[data file](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.csv) and
[metadata file](../resources/open-data-standards/pupil-enrolments.meta.csv).

The scripts are written for this example. Your own data is likely to have other
categories and missing or suppressed values that they do not handle.

If you don't use R or Python, you can reshape data in Excel using Power Query's
"Unpivot columns", or in SQL. Writing the steps as code means you can rerun
them for each release, see the
[RAP guidance on preparing data](../RAP/rap-statistics/rap-statistics-preparing-data.qmd).

## Check your files

EES runs the data screening checks automatically when you upload a data file
and metadata file. You can also run the same checks earlier in your own process
using either:

- the [EES data screener app](https://rsconnect/rsc/dfe-published-data-qa/),
  available on DfE kit
- the [eesyscreener](https://github.com/dfe-analytical-services/eesyscreener) R
  package, which you can add to your own pipeline

Fix any problems in your source data or code and regenerate the files, rather
than editing the CSVs by hand. Look at warnings as well as errors.

## Check how it looks in EES

After [uploading your files](ees.qmd#uploading-files), preview the release and
try the questions your users are likely to ask. For this example you might:

- make a table comparing male and female primary pupils across regions
- make a chart of percentages and check the labels, units and decimal places
- check that the default selections make sense
- set up featured tables to replace the tables you used to publish

For an existing publication, read the guidance on
[replacing data](ees.qmd#replacing-data) before changing column names or
structure, as this can break existing tables and charts.

If you plan to publish through the API, follow the
[API publishing checklist](api-data-standards.qmd#api-publishing-checklist).

## Checklists {#checklists}

### For each data file and metadata file

- [ ] The data is in a [tidy structure](ud.qmd#tidy-data-structure), with clear filters and indicators
- [ ] The [mandatory time and geography columns](ud.qmd#time-and-geography) are present
- [ ] Column names follow the [naming standards](ud.qmd#variable-names) and [harmonised variables](ud.qmd#common-harmonised-variables) are used where they apply
- [ ] Missing and suppressed values use the [standard symbols](ud.qmd#data-symbols)
- [ ] The metadata file has [all mandatory columns](ud.qmd#mandatory-ees-metadata-columns), matching column names and readable labels
- [ ] Both files are [UTF-8 CSVs](ud.qmd#data-format) with matching file names
- [ ] Both files pass the [screening checks](ud.qmd#how-to-check-against-these-standards)

### For the whole publication

- [ ] Data is split into files that make sense to compare, with as few files as practical
- [ ] Featured tables are set up for the views users need most often
- [ ] Everything in the data files meets your disclosure control policy
- [ ] [Public data guidance](ees.qmd#public-data-guidance) and methodology explain what each file contains
- [ ] Tables, charts and default selections have been checked in the EES preview
- [ ] If publishing through the API, the [API publishing checklist](api-data-standards.qmd#api-publishing-checklist) is complete

## Getting help

To upload and publish data you need access to the EES admin system, see
[accessing EES](ees.qmd#accessing-ees). For questions about data standards or
EES, contact the explore education statistics platforms team at
[explore.statistics@education.gov.uk](mailto:explore.statistics@education.gov.uk).
